steps.text:
You have played 1871 Caro-Kanns in these games. Almost all of them fall into three families, and you can tell which one you are in from a single question:

What did White do with the e4 pawn on move three?

Pushed it: the Advance. White's pawns on d4 and e5 lock the centre and point at your kingside. You have played this 532 times and scored 49%.

The plan in one line: attack d4, the base of the chain.

Traded it: the Exchange. No chain, open files. You have played it 483 times and scored 51%. If White follows up with c4 it becomes the Panov, which has its own lesson in the Openings group.

It also arrives without d4: after Nf3 or Bc4 and then exd5 cxd5, the pawns look the same and the same ideas apply.

The plan in one line: queenside. Rooks to the c- and b-files, and the b-pawn forward.

Defended it with a knight: you take. Nc3 (or Nd2) dxe4 Nxe4. Strictly this family is called the main line; the "Classical" is the name for Bf5 here.You never play Bf5. You play Nf6, 141 times, scoring 46%. That is your weakest Caro, so it gets its own lesson below. The engine rates the two moves the same (about a quarter of a pawn for White either way), so the move is not the problem.

Why it matters which one you are in: the same move can be right in one and wrong in another. Trading your light-squared bishop for the knight on f3 is a good idea in the Advance, because that knight guards d4. In the other two it is just a trade.

Which family, then which plan. The next card is what your games say about each.

The short answer: you do not make more mistakes in the Caro than players at your level. What costs you is two specific set-ups by White, and one family of moves.

A "big mistake" here means one move that drops your winning chance by 15 points or more out of 100. In the middle of the game (moves 13 to 30) you make 8.4 per 100 moves in the Advance and 8.5 in the Exchange. Fifteen players at your rating, in their own Caro games, make 9.8 and 10.4. So you are, if anything, slightly cleaner.

Where you lose ground:Your 4...Nf6 line. 46% from 141 games. You are already slightly behind by move 10 (your average winning chance 44 out of 100) and it keeps slipping (39 by move 25). It also has your highest opening mistake rate: 5.5 per 100 moves, against 4.0 in the Advance and 3.3 in the Exchange.The Exchange when White plays c3. 137 games, 45%. Your winning chance goes from 45 to 37 between moves 12 and 25. Against the knight on c3 instead: 379 games, 52%. Same-rated opponents in both, and you are not making more mistakes per move against c3. White is simply playing a set-up with a clear plan, and you need one too.The Advance with 4.dxc5. 30 games, 42%, and you are behind by move 12 (38). A small sample, but the games share a pattern, covered in the Advance lesson.

The moves that go wrong: pawn moves that open lines.

Kingside pawn moves (any move of your f-, g- or h-pawn that is not a capture) are a big mistake 12% of the time, against 7% for everything else. That is true at your level generally (the fifteen players: 12% against 8%), and you play them no more often than they do. So it is not a flaw of yours. It is the most dangerous move in this opening, for everyone.

Two central pawn pushes are as risky: d4 in the Advance (a big mistake in 26% of your 114 tries) and e5 in the Exchange (27% of 93). Peers are about the same.

Where you do look worse than peers, on small samples: f6 in the Advance (22% against 12%) and g5 in the Advance (26% against 6%).

Where the damage lands: 40% of your big mistakes are answered by a check or a move right next to your king. Peers: 36 to 39%. Again the opening, not you: the Caro sends the light-squared bishop out early, and it often gets traded, so your castled king has one defender fewer than in most openings.So what to do. Learn the plan for the two set-ups that hurt (the next three lessons), and treat every kingside pawn move as a move that needs a reason. The "Good idea or mistake?" deck is your own positions where you played exactly those moves.How sure is this? Exploratory: nothing here was predicted in advance, and the peer samples for single moves are small (13 to 40 moves). The 4...Nf6 and c3 results come from your games alone, 137 to 141 games each, so a difference of a few percent could be luck; the drift in winning chance is the steadier signal.

cards.sub: where it goes wrong, and where it doesn't

steps.text:
White's method: a pawn chain d4 and e5. It gives White space on the kingside, and against that you have one target: d4, the base of the chain.

You know the moves (the Openings group has them): c5, Nc6, Bg4 to remove d4's defender, e6, the knight to f5 and the queen to b6. You score 44% against c3 and 56% against Nf3, and you are usually better after move 12. That is the part to keep.

The idea that ties your mistakes together: your d5 and e6 pawns are walls. Behind them sits your king, and in front of them White's pieces are pointed at your position.

This is your game. You traded the bishop for the knight (fine), White took with the queen, then gave up the bishop on c6. Now the queen on f3 looks down the long diagonal, and the only thing between it and c6 is your d5 pawn.

You played d4, hitting the knight. The wall moved and Qxc6 was mate.

Bxc5 takes your pawn back and you would have been better. Nothing complicated was missed. A pawn that was blocking a line stopped blocking it.

The other wall: f7. The pawn on f7 guards two squares, e6 and g6. Play f6 and both lose their guard.

Another of your games. White's queen has just come to g4.

a6d3.note: Either keeps the walls up. In the game you played f6, and Qxe6+ won the pawn with check and the bishop on a6 next.

g8h8.note: That is fine too. The repertoire move here is Bd3. Either keeps the walls up. In the game you played f6, and Qxe6+ won the pawn with check and the bishop on a6 next.

steps.ask: Your move. Find something safe here.

bad.f7f6: That takes f7's guard off e6: Qxe6+ wins a pawn with check, and the bishop on a6 hangs next.

steps.hint: The queen on g4 is aimed at e6 and g7. Do not loosen either.

steps.text:
When is ...f6 right? When it hits e5 and the squares it gives up are covered: your king is not castled on that side yet, or e6 is defended by a piece and nothing of White's can reach g6. Then ...f6 opens the f-file for your rook, which is the other way to attack the chain.

The test before any f-, g- or h-pawn move: which square does this pawn stop guarding, and can a White piece get there?

Against 4.dxc5. White gives up the chain to grab a pawn. You have answered Nc6 almost every time, and you score 42% here.

The cleaner move is e6, and the bishop takes back on c5. The pawn comes back, the bishop is on a good diagonal, and you never needed the knight on c6, which is exactly where the queen-and-bishop tricks above land.

b8c6.note: That is fine too. The repertoire move here is e6. Then Bxc5. Nc6 is playable too, but it puts a knight on the square White's bishop and queen are aiming at.

e7e6.note: Then Bxc5. Nc6 is playable too, but it puts a knight on the square White's bishop and queen are aiming at.

steps.hint: Get the pawn back with a piece that wants to be on c5.

steps.text: One more thing from your trade check: in the Advance you are usually a little better after move 12, and that is where your even trades handed the edge back. Before trading in the Advance, ask whether your pieces are doing more than White's. They usually are.

cards.t: The Advance: walls and the d4 target

steps.text: Two White set-ups. With the knight on c3 the position stays symmetrical and you do fine: 52% from 379 games. With the pawn on c3 and the bishop on d3, White has a plan, and you score 45% from 137 games, sliding from a 45 to a 37 winning chance between moves 12 and 25.

White's plan: the kingside. Bishop on d3, queen to c2, knight to e5, sometimes f4, all aimed at h7. In your c3 games White put a knight on e5 in 41%% and the bishop on d3 in 43%%, twice as often as in the other Exchange games.Your plan: the queenside. Bishop out, castle, rooks to c8 and b8, then b5 and b4 to hit the pawn on c3. When it goes, White is left with a weak pawn on c3 or d4 and you have an open file. You already push the b-pawn in half these games. Good.

The race means h7 needs a guard. Your light-squared bishop often leaves for f3 (it is a fine trade), and then the knight on f6 is h7's only defender. When that knight moves or is traded, h7 is the first thing to look at.

Your game: White has just recaptured on h5 with the queen.

g7g6.note: Blocks the bishop and takes the queen's squares. In the game Bxg5 was met by Qxh7 mate.

bad.e7g5: Qxh7 is mate. The knight that guarded h7 was traded on h5.

steps.hint: Count what hits h7, and what defends it.

steps.text:
The other risky move: e5. It looks active, but it opens the e-file and leaves your d5 pawn alone in the middle. In your Exchange games it was a big mistake 27% of the time (93 tries). Peers: about the same. Only push it when d5 is solidly covered and nothing is lined up on the e-file.

Your game: rooks are on the c-file and your knights are active. You played e5, and Nxd5 simply took the pawn.

e4d6.note: Keep the pressure on c3 and leave d5 where it is. That is the queenside plan working: White's pawns on c3 and a4 are the targets.

e8d8.note: That is fine too. The repertoire move here is Nd6. Keep the pressure on c3 and leave d5 where it is. That is the queenside plan working: White's pawns on c3 and a4 are the targets.

bad.e6e5: Nxd5. The pawn on d5 lost the e6 pawn's support.

steps.hint: Look at what White's c3 and a4 pawns need.

steps.text: In one line: against c3 and Bd3, push on the queenside, keep a guard on h7, and leave your e- and kingside pawns alone until there is a reason. Against Qb3 early, Qd7 (it is in the Openings group).

cards.sub: a queenside plan against a kingside one
cards.t: The Exchange: when White plays c3

steps.text: After Nxe4 Nf6, White almost always takes: Nxf6+, and you take back towards the middle with exf6. White took in 77 of your 141 games here, and you recaptured with the e-pawn every time.

Read the pawns. On the queenside White has four pawns (a, b, c, d) against your three. On the kingside you have four against three, but two of yours are doubled, so they cannot make a passed pawn.

That means one thing: endgames favour White. With the queens off, White's extra queenside pawn eventually becomes a passed pawn and yours never will. So you want pieces on the board and quick development. This is the one Caro line where your habit of taking every even trade is wrong.
The set-up: Bd6, castle, rook to e8, and then the knight goes the long way: d7, f8, and on to g6 or e6.

d7f8.note: The knight on f8 guards h7 for good, and from there it reaches g6 and e6. This is the standard regrouping in this line, and the engine's top choice here.

h7h6.note: That is fine too. The repertoire move here is Nf8. The knight on f8 guards h7 for good, and from there it reaches g6 and e6. This is the standard regrouping in this line, and the engine's top choice here.

steps.ask: White has lined up the bishop and queen on h7. Your move.
steps.hint: One of your pieces can cover h7 permanently.

steps.text:
Your f6 pawn helps too: it keeps White's knight off e5 and g5. That is why this structure holds up.

Two warnings from your games. Pushing your kingside pawns strips the king: g5 was a big mistake in 33% of your 30 tries in this line. And the bishop sacrifice on h7 appears in game after game when h7 has no knight next to it. Get the knight to f8 before anything else on the kingside.
If White does not take on f6: Ng5 has its own card in the Openings group (h6, kick it at once). Ng3 is answered by normal development: Bg4 or Bf5, e6, Bd6 or Be7.
